title: Garlic-Cream Pommes Purée
description: Robuchon-style mashed potatoes with garlic-steeped cream beaten in — the purée IS the sauce.
source: Developed with the chef, cooked 2026-09-07 (artichoke night)

changelog.note: First publish — from the no-protein artichoke night. Cooked peeled that night; skins-on is the canonical method, rescue note included.

steps.text: Put the 2½ lb potatoes — whole, skins on — in cold, well-salted water. Bring to a gentle boil and cook about 25 minutes, until a knife slides out with no grip.
steps.why: The skins keep water out of the flesh while it cooks. Dry potato is what makes room for a stick of butter — waterlogged potato rejects it and turns gluey.

steps.text: While they boil: put the 12 smashed garlic cloves and 1½ cups heavy cream at the barest simmer for 12 minutes, until a clove mashes against the pan wall with no resistance. Mash them all into the cream right in the pot, lid on, off heat.
steps.why: Steeping mellows the garlic from sharp to sweet, and the cream carries it evenly through the purée instead of in hot pockets.

steps.text: Cube the 2 sticks of butter and put them back in the fridge until needed.
steps.why: Cold butter absorbs in stages and emulsifies; soft butter just melts into a grease slick. Cold is not optional.

steps.text: Drain the potatoes and peel them scorching hot — towel in one hand, paring knife in the other; the skins slip right off. Rice them back into the dry, empty pot.
Stir the riced potatoes over low heat 2 to 3 minutes to steam off surface moisture.
steps.why: This drying pass is what saves the texture — every bit of water driven off now is room for fat later.

steps.text: On the lowest heat, beat in the 16 tbsp of cold butter in 4 to 5 additions, each fully absorbed before the next. The mixture must never come close to a simmer.

Beat in the warm garlic cream in stages, by feel — stop when the purée slumps slowly off a spoon like thick paint. You may not need all 1½ cups. Taste, then season with fine salt, and the white pepper and nutmeg whisper if you like.
Hold on the lowest flame with the lid on, stirring occasionally, up to 20 minutes.
steps.why: A deep mass of purée catches on the pot floor sooner than you expect — the occasional stir is cheap insurance.

notes.title: If you peeled first
notes.body: Recoverable. Drop the boil to a gentle simmer (a hard boil batters and waterlogs bare potatoes), stretch the drying pass to a full 4–5 minutes — until the steam slows and the mass films the pot floor — add the cream more cautiously, and taste before salting: peeled potatoes drink salt from the water.

notes.title: The one rule
notes.body: Nothing above a simmer once butter is in. Gluey purée and broken sauce live at the same temperature — low and slow is the whole religion.

notes.title: Leftovers
notes.body: Reheats over low heat with a splash of cream, good as new the next day.

plating: Warm shallow bowls, a big spoonful swooshed off-center with the back of the spoon — it should hold the swoosh. Whatever it accompanies leans against it.
elevations: A few drops of lemon juice at the end — fat mutes, acid restores.
Snipped chives over the top for color and bite.
Full Robuchon: push the butter toward 3 sticks and pass the purée through a fine sieve for silk.
pairings: Anything seared with a pan sauce
variations: Making the steamed artichokes too? Steep once for both: 14 cloves in 2 cups cream, reserve ½ cup for the dip before the purée gets the rest.
